name: A Peace I Can't Explain
description: Fourteen days to name the anxiety, bring it to God, and learn to breathe inside it.

days.openingPrayer: God, before I go anywhere today — I notice what I'm carrying. Meet me here.

scripture.verseText: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.

days.practicalMeaning:
Paul is writing this from a prison cell. He isn't telling people who feel anxious to stop feeling it — he's telling them where to bring it. Anxiety, in his framing, isn't a sin or a weakness. It's a signal: something matters, and you don't know how to carry it alone.

The instruction is small but radical. In every thing — not just the big things — let your requests be made known. Pair the asking with thanksgiving, because thanksgiving keeps you from being swallowed by the fear. And the result isn't that your circumstances change. The result is a peace that doesn't make sense given what you're facing.
days.smallAction: Today, the next time you feel anxiety rise, name it out loud (or in a whisper) as a one-sentence prayer. Not a plan, not a solution — just naming it to God.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where in your body did you first notice anxiety today? What was the trigger — even if it seems small?

quiz.question: What does Paul invite us to do "in every thing"?
quiz.explanation: Paul doesn't say not to feel anxiety. He says where to bring it — to God, in prayer, with thanksgiving alongside the request.

days.themeLabel: He is in the storm with you
days.openingPrayer: Jesus, when the boat is rocking I forget you're already in it. Wake me up to your presence.

scripture.verseText: And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish? And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

days.practicalMeaning: The disciples weren't faithless for being afraid — there was a real storm. What they got wrong was assuming Jesus didn't care because he was asleep. Anxiety often makes us read God's quietness as absence. It rarely is. Sometimes the calm comes when he speaks; sometimes the calm is that he was there the whole time.
days.smallAction: Today, when anxiety spikes, say silently: "You're already in the boat." Don't try to feel it — just say it.
days.reflectionPrompt: When did God's silence today feel like absence? What might it have actually been?

quiz.question: What did the disciples assume about Jesus's sleep?
options: That he didn't care if they perished
quiz.explanation: Their fear made them read his quiet as not caring. He was present the whole time.

days.themeLabel: It was never yours to carry alone
days.openingPrayer: God, I've been holding this like it's mine to fix. Help me set it down.

scripture.verseText: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.

days.practicalMeaning: Peter uses a deliberate word: cast. Not hand over politely — throw. The instruction assumes you've been gripping something tightly. The reason it's safe to throw it is the second half of the sentence: he careth for you. Not your performance, your competence, your readiness. You.
days.smallAction: Write down one thing you've been gripping. Then write below it: "This is not mine to carry alone." Re-read it three times today.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's the thing you keep picking back up after you set it down?

quiz.question: Peter says to cast our cares because…
options: It's the strong thing to do
quiz.explanation: The basis isn't willpower. It's that he cares for you, personally — so it's safe to throw, not just hand over.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, the peace I keep trying to manufacture doesn't hold. Give me the kind that does.

scripture.verseText: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.

days.practicalMeaning: The world's peace is conditional: solve the problem, remove the threat, fix the relationship. Jesus offers something different — a peace that holds while the problem is still unsolved. That's the only kind that actually works in anxious times, because anxious times rarely cooperate with our solving.
days.smallAction: Notice one moment today where you tried to manufacture peace by fixing a thing. Pause and ask: can I sit here, unfixed, for sixty seconds?
days.reflectionPrompt: What did you try to fix today that wasn't yours to fix?

quiz.question: How is Jesus's peace different from the world's?
options: It holds while circumstances don't change
quiz.explanation: The world's peace needs the threat to go away. His holds before the threat goes away — sometimes whether or not it does.

days.openingPrayer: God, I want to understand before I trust. Help me trust before I understand.

scripture.verseText: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

days.practicalMeaning: Anxiety often demands a map before a step. Proverbs flips the order: take the step, then the path gets clearer. "Lean not unto thine own understanding" isn't anti-intellectual — it's anti-paralysis. Your understanding is real, just not load-bearing enough for the future.
days.smallAction: Identify one decision you've been delaying until you understand it fully. Take the smallest possible next step on it today.
days.reflectionPrompt: What are you waiting to understand before you'll trust?

quiz.question: What does the verse warn against leaning on?
quiz.explanation: Not because understanding is bad — because it isn't strong enough on its own to direct the path.

days.openingPrayer: God, I confuse stillness with giving up. Teach me the difference.

scripture.verseText: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.

days.practicalMeaning: "Be still" isn't a suggestion to relax — the Hebrew word is closer to "let your hands drop." Stop the gripping, the fixing, the controlling. In an anxious mind, stillness feels like negligence. It isn't. It's an active refusal to keep performing what only God can carry.
days.smallAction: Take ninety seconds today to sit with your hands open in your lap. Don't pray words — just keep your hands open.
days.reflectionPrompt: What does "letting your hands drop" cost you to do?

quiz.question: "Be still" in this verse means closest to…
quiz.explanation: The Hebrew is about releasing grip — letting your hands drop — not just feeling calm.

days.openingPrayer: God, my fear keeps telling me a story. Speak a truer one over me today.

scripture.verseText: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.

days.practicalMeaning: Notice the sequence: don't be afraid, because I am with you. Not because the danger is fake or the strength is in you — because of presence. Anxiety tells a story where you're alone with the threat. This verse tells a truer one.
days.smallAction: When fear rises today, finish this sentence in your head: "I'm afraid of ___, and God is with me anyway." Hold both halves.
days.reflectionPrompt: What story is your fear telling you? What's the truer one?

quiz.question: Why does the verse say "fear not"?
quiz.explanation: The reason isn't denial of danger or self-sufficiency — it's the company of God.

days.openingPrayer: God, you give bread for today. Help me stop trying to eat tomorrow's.

scripture.verseText: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

days.practicalMeaning: Jesus isn't saying don't plan — he's saying don't pre-suffer. Anxiety is the practice of carrying tomorrow's possible weight today, in a body designed for one day at a time. "Sufficient unto the day" is permission to put down everything that isn't today's.
days.smallAction: Catch yourself in one piece of pre-suffering today. Say: "That's tomorrow's. I'm not equipped for it today on purpose."
days.reflectionPrompt: What were you carrying today that wasn't actually today's to carry?

quiz.question: What's Jesus telling us NOT to do?
quiz.explanation: The teaching isn't against planning — it's against carrying tomorrow's weight in today's body.

days.openingPrayer: God, in the swirl of what's wrong, help me see what's right enough to thank you for.

scripture.verseText: Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.

days.practicalMeaning: "In every thing give thanks" doesn't mean for every thing. It means inside every thing, find something. Gratitude is an anchor — it doesn't stop the storm, but it keeps you from drifting where you can't get back from.
days.smallAction: Before you sleep, write down three small things from today you can thank God for. Specific things. Not categories.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's the smallest thing today that you'd have missed thanking God for?

quiz.question: Give thanks…
quiz.explanation: The preposition matters. Not for — in. There's almost always something inside the moment worth naming.

days.openingPrayer: Spirit, when I can't find words, pray inside me.

scripture.verseText: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God.

days.practicalMeaning: There are days when anxiety steals the words. Paul says: that's fine. The Spirit prays inside you with groans that don't translate. You don't have to find the right words — you have to be willing to be prayed for from the inside out.
days.smallAction: When you can't pray today, just breathe slowly four times and say once: "Spirit, pray in me." That counts.
days.reflectionPrompt: When today did you feel like your prayers were too small? What might have been praying for you?

quiz.question: What does the Spirit do when we don't know how to pray?
options: Waits for us to figure it out
Prays inside us with wordless groans
quiz.explanation: Wordlessness isn't a barrier. The Spirit prays underneath your words when you don't have them.

days.openingPrayer: God, my mind has grooves I keep falling into. Re-groove me.

scripture.verseText: And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.

days.practicalMeaning: Anxious thought patterns are real grooves in the brain — well-worn paths. Paul's word is "transformed" (metamorphoō), the same word for a caterpillar becoming something else entirely. The renewal isn't decoration. It's structural, and it happens by exposure to what's true, repeatedly, over time.
days.smallAction: Pick one anxious thought you've had this week. Write the true thing next to it. Re-read both tomorrow morning.
days.reflectionPrompt: What groove in your thinking do you most need re-cut?

quiz.question: The Greek word for "transformed" is the same word for…
quiz.explanation: Metamorphoō — structural change, not redecoration. The renewal is deep.

days.openingPrayer: God, hope feels naive some days. Help me practice it anyway.

scripture.verseText: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

days.practicalMeaning: Hope isn't a feeling. It's a posture — choosing to lean toward something you can't yet see. Anxiety wants you to require proof before you'll lean. Faith says: leaning is the proof. The muscle gets stronger by being used in the dark.
days.smallAction: Name one thing you're hoping for that you can't see proof of yet. Lean toward it today in one specific way.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where today did you ask for proof when you could have practiced hope instead?

quiz.question: Faith is described as the…
quiz.explanation: Substance — something real, weight-bearing. Not a feeling, but a posture toward what isn't yet visible.

days.themeLabel: We were not built to carry alone
days.openingPrayer: God, the part of me that won't ask for help is also the part that's drowning. Soften it.

scripture.verseText: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

days.practicalMeaning: Anxiety isolates. The shame around it whispers: don't tell anyone how heavy this is. Paul says the law of Christ is fulfilled when burdens get shared. Telling one person today isn't weakness — it's the practice that breaks the isolation.
days.smallAction: Tell one person — text, call, in-person — something honest about what you've been carrying. Not the whole thing. Just one true sentence.
days.reflectionPrompt: Who came to mind just now? What stops you from telling them?

quiz.question: Bearing one another's burdens fulfills…
quiz.explanation: It's not optional kindness — Paul calls it the actual fulfillment of Christ's way.

days.openingPrayer: God, thank you for these fourteen days. Carry me into the next fourteen the same way.

scripture.verseText: And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.

days.practicalMeaning: We end where we started — but you're not the same person who started. "Passeth all understanding" means peace doesn't wait for you to figure it out. It guards your heart and mind in the figuring. The work of these days wasn't to remove anxiety; it was to teach you where to bring it.
days.smallAction: Look back at what you wrote on day 1. Then write one sentence to your day-1 self about what you've learned.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's different about how you're holding anxiety today than fourteen days ago?

quiz.question: The peace of God…
quiz.explanation: It surpasses — moves past — understanding. You don't have to figure it out for it to guard you.

name: Held Through the Grief
description: Fourteen quiet days to grieve without rushing, and to find God closer than the pain.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, you wept. Teach me to weep without apologizing for it.

scripture.verseText: Jesus wept.

days.practicalMeaning: Two of the shortest words in scripture, and they reshape everything. Jesus knew he was about to raise Lazarus. He still wept. The grief was honored before the miracle. That means you don't need to skip your weeping to get to your healing. The tears are part of how you love what you lost.
days.smallAction: If tears come today, let them. Don't apologize, don't explain. Just notice that Jesus did this too.
days.reflectionPrompt: What part of your grief have you been treating like a problem to solve instead of love to honor?

quiz.question: Why does Jesus's weeping matter here?
options: Because he didn't know what to do
Because grief is honored even when healing is coming
Because he forgot Lazarus would rise
quiz.explanation: He knew the miracle was minutes away. He wept anyway — because grief is honored, not bypassed.

days.openingPrayer: God, when I feel furthest from you, help me know you're closest.

scripture.verseText: The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

days.practicalMeaning: Grief often feels like God left the room. The Psalmist says the opposite — broken-heartedness is exactly where God comes near. Not despite the brokenness. Because of it. Whatever you're feeling that you think disqualifies you from God's presence is the thing drawing him close.
days.smallAction: Sit somewhere quiet for two minutes today and say: "You are near to me here." That's enough.
days.reflectionPrompt: What did you assume your grief was keeping you from? What might it actually be?

quiz.question: When does the verse say the Lord is near?
quiz.explanation: The brokenness isn't a barrier — it's the gathering place.

days.openingPrayer: God, you keep track of what feels too small to name. Thank you.

scripture.verseText: Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?

days.practicalMeaning: David is asking God to collect his tears in a bottle. The image is strange and beautiful — that nothing of your sorrow is wasted on God. He doesn't just see; he saves. The grief you can't even articulate is being counted, kept, honored by the one who made you.
days.smallAction: Name one tear-worthy thing from this week — even quietly to yourself. It's been counted.
days.reflectionPrompt: What loss have you been treating as too small to mention? What if it isn't?

quiz.question: What does the verse say God does with our tears?
quiz.explanation: The image is preservation, not erasure. Nothing of your sorrow is wasted on God.

days.themeLabel: The night does not last forever
days.openingPrayer: God, the night feels longer than I can carry. Help me trust morning is still coming.

scripture.verseText: Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.

days.practicalMeaning: This isn't a promise that grief is short. It's a promise that grief is not the end. "Weeping may endure for a night" — and some nights are years. But morning is in the architecture of how God built things. Joy is not the absence of what you lost; it's the surprise of being able to feel light again, eventually.
days.smallAction: When the night feels heaviest today, whisper: "This is the night. Morning is still part of the story."
days.reflectionPrompt: What does your imagination tell you about your future? What truer thing could you tell yourself instead?

quiz.question: What is the verse promising about morning?
options: Joy is in the design — it returns
We must believe to feel joy
quiz.explanation: It's not a timeline. It's a structure: morning comes because of how this was built.

days.openingPrayer: God, you made time for weeping. Help me stop fighting that.

scripture.verseText: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance.

days.practicalMeaning: Ecclesiastes refuses to skip the hard half. Mourning isn't a season to apologize for or accelerate. It has its own time, its own dignity, its own purpose. The wisdom is in not insisting on dancing when it's still time to weep — and not insisting on weeping when, eventually, dancing has come back.
days.smallAction: Notice what time it is in your grief today. Mourning? Quiet? Confused? Whatever it is, let it be that.
days.reflectionPrompt: What season are you in? What would honoring it look like today?

quiz.question: What does Ecclesiastes teach about grief's time?
options: It has its own time and dignity
It must end before you can heal
quiz.explanation: Mourning is named alongside dancing. They're both seasons. Neither needs to apologize.

days.themeLabel: Hope when you can't feel it
days.openingPrayer: God, the mercies feel far today. Help me trust they're new even when I can't see them.

scripture.verseText: It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

days.practicalMeaning: Lamentations doesn't sugarcoat — it's literally a book of weeping. And in the middle of it, this. Not "the pain is gone" but "we are not consumed." Survival itself is mercy. And the mercy is fresh every morning — you don't have to ration what's already been given.
days.smallAction: Notice one mercy you survived on today. Coffee. Sleep. A friend's text. Any of it counts.
days.reflectionPrompt: What got you through today, even in a small way? Whose mercy was that?

quiz.question: How often does the verse say mercies come?
quiz.explanation: Every morning. You don't have to stockpile — there's always more.

days.themeLabel: Comfort that becomes ours to give
days.openingPrayer: God, the comfort you've given me will one day be something I give. Make me ready for that.

scripture.verseText: Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul's logic is hard but true: the comfort you receive in grief becomes, eventually, comfort you can give to someone else. Your loss is not wasted. It's not the meaning of the loss — but it's part of the redemption of it. The person who'll need you in two years can only be reached by someone who's been where you are.
days.smallAction: Think of one person who's grieving. You don't have to fix anything — just hold them in mind today.
days.reflectionPrompt: Who do you know that's where you were three months ago? What would you say to them now?

quiz.question: What does Paul say comfort eventually becomes?
quiz.explanation: Comfort given becomes comfort to give. Your grief, in time, becomes someone's lifeline.

days.openingPrayer: God, today is all you've given me. Help me not carry tomorrow's grief on top of it.

scripture.verseText: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

days.practicalMeaning: Grief is exhausting partly because it tries to project itself forward — "every birthday, every anniversary, every Christmas, forever." Jesus draws the line at today. You have strength for today's grief. You don't have strength for next year's, and you weren't supposed to. The grace will be there when you arrive.
days.smallAction: When grief catches you imagining the future, gently bring it back: "Just today. That's all I need to carry."
days.reflectionPrompt: Which future grief have you been trying to pre-mourn? What if you put it down until then?

quiz.question: What is Jesus telling us about grief and tomorrow?
quiz.explanation: Today has enough. Tomorrow's grace will be there when tomorrow comes.

days.openingPrayer: God, even my asking where you are is a kind of prayer. Hear it.

scripture.verseText: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.

days.practicalMeaning: This is in the Bible. This is in the prayer book of the people of God. The cry of feeling abandoned is so welcome in scripture that Jesus quoted it from the cross. If you've been hiding the part of your grief that questions where God is, you can stop hiding. It's already on the page. It's already a prayer.
days.smallAction: Say it out loud: "My God, where are you?" That's not unbelief. That's prayer.
days.reflectionPrompt: What part of your grief have you been editing out of your prayers? What would happen if you let it in?

quiz.question: Who quoted Psalm 22:1 in their own grief?
quiz.explanation: Jesus prayed this. The cry of forsakenness is part of the language of faith, not a failure of it.

days.openingPrayer: Shepherd, I'm in the valley. I don't need it removed. I need you in it.

scripture.verseText: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.

days.practicalMeaning: Notice what David doesn't ask for. He doesn't ask to skip the valley. He walks through it. The fearlessness isn't from the valley being short or shallow — it's from the company. "Thou art with me" is the whole sentence. Everything else is a footnote.
days.smallAction: When you feel the valley deepest today, say: "You are with me." Five words. That's enough.
days.reflectionPrompt: What would change about today if you actually trusted that you weren't walking it alone?

quiz.question: What makes David unafraid in the valley?
quiz.explanation: Presence, not removal. The valley still exists — he just isn't alone in it.

days.openingPrayer: God, give me eyes to see what's already been given.

scripture.verseText: It is of the Lord's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

days.practicalMeaning: We return to this verse on purpose. Grief makes us forget how we got from yesterday to today. The act of looking back and noticing — "those were mercies, that was kindness, this was provision" — slowly rebuilds the floor under your faith. Faithfulness isn't a feeling. It's a track record you can look at.
days.smallAction: Look back at this week. Name three small mercies. Write them down if you can.
days.reflectionPrompt: What mercies did you almost miss because the grief was loud?

quiz.question: How do we rebuild trust in God's faithfulness?
options: By trying harder to feel it
quiz.explanation: Faithfulness is a pattern you can look back at. Naming it builds floor underneath.

days.openingPrayer: God, take what feels like only loss and make it grow into something.

scripture.verseText: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

days.practicalMeaning: The Psalmist watches farmers walk into the fields weeping during a famine, knowing they're planting their last grain. He says: those tears are not wasted. The same tears that fall onto the seed will be there when the harvest comes. Grief is not loss without meaning. It's slow, hidden, certain planting.
days.smallAction: Acknowledge today that the weeping you've done is doing something even when you can't see it.
days.reflectionPrompt: What might be quietly growing in you because of what you've lost?

quiz.question: What does the verse promise about tears?
quiz.explanation: The tears are part of the planting. The harvest isn't despite them — it's because of them.

days.openingPrayer: God, I don't want to skip the sorrow. I want hope inside it.

scripture.verseText: But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul doesn't say "don't sorrow." He says "don't sorrow as those who have no hope." Christian grief is still grief — full, real, sometimes ugly. The difference isn't the absence of tears; it's the presence of a thread. You're not pretending. You're grieving with a thread of "and this isn't the end" running underneath.
days.smallAction: Hold both today: the sorrow is real, and the hope is real. Don't pick one. Carry both.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where have you felt pressure to choose between grief and hope? What if you don't have to?

quiz.question: How does Paul describe Christian grief?
quiz.explanation: Both, at once. The grief is honored; the hope is the thread underneath that won't snap.

days.openingPrayer: God, take what's been left as ashes. Slowly, gently, make something.

scripture.verseText: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn; To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness.

days.practicalMeaning: Fourteen days end where Isaiah and Jesus both begin: with the mission to comfort those who mourn. "Beauty for ashes" isn't a swap that erases what was burned. The ashes are still there — but something has grown in them. You won't have the version of life you had before. You'll have a different beauty. Hard-won. Quieter. Truer.
days.smallAction: Look back at day 1 and your first reflection. Then write one sentence to your day-1 self about what you've learned to carry.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's different about how you're holding this grief today than fourteen days ago?

quiz.question: What does "beauty for ashes" mean?
options: Beauty grows in what was burned
quiz.explanation: Not erasure — growth. The ashes are still there, and something new is rising from them.

name: Do I Know Jesus?
description: Fourteen days for anyone new to faith — or returning. The basics, said honestly.

days.openingPrayer: God, if you are real, meet me here. I'm willing to start.

scripture.verseText: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

days.practicalMeaning: Faith starts here — not with a list of rules, but with a claim about reality. There is a beginning, and there is a beginner. The universe didn't make itself; it was made by Someone. That changes the question you're asking. The question is no longer "is anyone there?" but "who is the Someone who made this — and what is he like?"
days.smallAction: Look around once today and let yourself notice that everything you see was made. Just notice. Don't decide anything yet.
days.reflectionPrompt: What is the first thing that comes to mind when you imagine "God"? Where did that picture come from?

quiz.question: What's the first claim of the Bible?
quiz.explanation: Everything else flows from this. Before sin, before salvation — there's a Creator. The story starts with who he is.

days.openingPrayer: God, the thought that you actually know me is hard to hold. Help me sit with it.

scripture.verseText: O Lord, thou hast searched me, and known me. Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. Thou compassest my path, and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O Lord, thou knowest it altogether.

days.practicalMeaning: If God exists, the next question is: does he know me, or is he too big to bother? David's answer is: he knows you to a level that's almost uncomfortable. Sitting, standing, thinking, before you even speak. The God who made galaxies also knows your specific Tuesday. That's both terrifying and the most welcoming thing in the world.
days.smallAction: Pick one tiny thing about today — what you ate, who you texted, a thought you had — and say in your head, "You know this."
days.reflectionPrompt: Is it more comforting or unsettling that God might know you completely? Why?

quiz.question: What does this Psalm say about God's knowledge of us?
options: He knows what we do publicly
He knows everything — our thoughts, paths, words
He knows about us but isn't interested
He only knows the good things
quiz.explanation: It's total — thoughts before you speak them, paths before you walk them. Not surveillance. Knowing-as-love.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, you stepped into this. Let me see you, not just hear about you.

scripture.verseText: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

days.practicalMeaning: Christianity's wildest claim is this one: God didn't stay distant. He became a person — flesh, sweat, hunger, friends, tears. "Dwelt among us" literally means "pitched his tent." He moved into the neighborhood. Whatever you think faith is, it's not about climbing up to God. It's about a God who came down. That's why Jesus matters: he's God's face turned toward you.
days.smallAction: Say the name "Jesus" once, in your head or out loud. That's the doorway. You don't need anything else yet.
days.reflectionPrompt: What does it change if God isn't only distant power, but also a person who knows what it's like to be tired?

quiz.question: What does John 1:14 claim about Jesus?
options: God became flesh and lived among us
quiz.explanation: Not a wise man. Not a metaphor. God himself, in skin, with us. That's the claim Christianity stands or falls on.

days.openingPrayer: God, help me see myself the way you do.

scripture.verseText: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

days.practicalMeaning: Before the Bible talks about anything you've done wrong, it tells you who you are. You bear God's image. Not because of your performance, your beliefs, your morality — because he made you that way. Every person you've ever met, and yourself, walks around carrying something of God in them. That's the floor. Everything else is built on it.
days.smallAction: When you look in a mirror today, notice — even just once — that the face looking back is made in the image of God.
days.reflectionPrompt: What part of yourself have you been treating as worthless that God might be calling beloved?

quiz.question: When did humans receive God's image?
quiz.explanation: It's the starting condition, not a reward. You bear his image before you ever knew it.

days.openingPrayer: God, the idea that you loved me before I deserved it doesn't compute. Help me let it be true anyway.

scripture.verseText: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

days.practicalMeaning: Most love runs on a transaction: I love you because. God's runs the other way: I love you before. Paul wants this explicit — Jesus didn't die for the lovable, the cleaned-up, or the deserving. He died for people in the middle of their mess. If you've been waiting to feel worthy before approaching God, you've been waiting on the wrong condition. The worth was supplied. Yours is to receive.
days.smallAction: Write down one thing you've assumed disqualifies you from God's love. Then write next to it: "This is exactly when he loved me."
days.reflectionPrompt: What have you been waiting to fix about yourself before you'd be willing to be loved?

quiz.question: When did Christ die for us, according to Paul?
options: When we had cleaned up our lives
quiz.explanation: The love came first. The mess didn't disqualify you — it's the precise moment God chose.

days.openingPrayer: God, take the shame I've been carrying. I don't want to carry it past today.

scripture.verseText: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.

days.practicalMeaning: Most of us walk around with an inner voice that condemns. Paul says: for those in Christ, that voice isn't God's. The legal verdict has been delivered already, and it's "not guilty." The voice in your head saying you're too far gone, you've failed too much, you're a fraud — that voice is real, and it's not God's. Learning to tell them apart is most of the early work of faith.
days.smallAction: When the inner condemnation hits today, say back: "That is not God's voice over me."
days.reflectionPrompt: What's the most common condemning thought you have about yourself? What would the no-condemnation version sound like?

quiz.question: For those in Christ, what is the verdict?
quiz.explanation: The court has ruled. It's not provisional. The condemning voice in your head — whatever else it is — isn't the gavel of God.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, I want a way in. Be it for me.

scripture.verseText: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

days.practicalMeaning: This verse is famous, and often weaponized. Hear it gently: Jesus isn't saying "you have to be Christian enough to get in." He's saying "I am the door, and the door is open." The path to God isn't a list of religious requirements to satisfy. It's a person to receive. "By me" means he carries the weight you were never built to carry.
days.smallAction: Sit quietly for thirty seconds today and say: "Jesus, be my way." That counts. That's the door.
days.reflectionPrompt: What religious requirement have you been trying to satisfy? What if the requirement was already met for you?

quiz.question: What does Jesus mean by "I am the way"?
options: He's the way to God — a person to receive, not requirements to satisfy
quiz.explanation: A person, not a religion. A door, not a hurdle.

days.openingPrayer: God, I'll just talk to you. That's it.

scripture.verseText: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.

days.practicalMeaning: Jesus knew people would try to make prayer into a performance, so he said: go in the closet, shut the door. Prayer isn't volume, or vocabulary, or convincing words. It's a Father in the dark, listening to you. If you've been trying to pray and feeling like you don't know how — good. That's the right place to start. Plain words, in a quiet room, with the door shut.
days.smallAction: Find a quiet thirty seconds today. Say whatever's on your mind to God. No script. No performance.
days.reflectionPrompt: What have you been assuming prayer is supposed to sound like? Where did that assumption come from?

quiz.question: What's Jesus warning against in prayer?
quiz.explanation: Performance. Volume. The closet-with-the-door-shut prayer is the one he's pointing to.

days.themeLabel: When you don't know what to say
days.openingPrayer: Spirit, when I have no words, pray inside me.

scripture.verseText: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God.

days.practicalMeaning: The first weeks of faith are confusing. You'll sit down to pray and have no idea what to say. Paul writes: that's fine. The Spirit prays *inside* you. You don't have to find the right words. You have to be willing to let yourself be prayed for from the inside out. Sometimes the holiest prayer is sitting quietly with the sense that something good is praying for you.
days.smallAction: When you don't know what to pray today, just breathe slowly four times and say once: "Spirit, pray in me." That's the whole thing.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where today did you stop praying because you didn't know what to say? What if that wasn't the disqualifier you thought?

quiz.question: What does the Spirit do when we don't know how to pray?
options: Waits for us to figure it out
Prays inside us with wordless groans
quiz.explanation: The Spirit prays underneath your words when you don't have any. You're not alone in the silence.

days.openingPrayer: God, here's the small stuff. Here's the big stuff. All of it.

scripture.verseText: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.

days.practicalMeaning: Notice the scope: in every thing. Not just the spiritual things, not just the dignified things. The boring, the petty, the embarrassing, the ones you think God shouldn't have to deal with. Paul says give him all of it. Pair the asking with thanksgiving — it keeps you from being swallowed by what you're asking about. The peace isn't promised because the problem got solved. It's promised because you stopped carrying it alone.
days.smallAction: Pray about something today you'd normally think is "too small" for God. He cares.
days.reflectionPrompt: What have you been refusing to bring to God because you assumed it was beneath his attention?

quiz.question: What does Paul say to bring to God?
quiz.explanation: Every thing. The bar is low on purpose.

days.openingPrayer: Father, teach me to pray your way.

scripture.verseText: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread.

days.practicalMeaning: Jesus's disciples asked for one thing: teach us to pray. He gave them this. Notice what's in it: who God is, what we long for him to do, what we need today, the asking for forgiveness, the asking not to be tested past what we can bear. It's a template, not a magic spell. Pray it slowly today, line by line. It will teach you more than a hundred books about prayer.
days.smallAction: Pray Matthew 6:9-13 once today, slowly. Pause on the line that catches you.
days.reflectionPrompt: Which line of the Lord's Prayer most hits you today? Why that one?

quiz.question: What is the Lord's Prayer?
options: A template Jesus gave for how to pray
The only prayer we can pray
quiz.explanation: A template. The disciples asked how to pray; he showed them. Use the bones, fill in your own words.

days.openingPrayer: God, I'd rather understand. Help me trust anyway.

scripture.verseText: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

days.practicalMeaning: Faith isn't certainty. It isn't the absence of questions. It's the substance — something real and weight-bearing — of what you hope for, even when you can't see it yet. Plenty of people who've believed for decades still have questions. They just learned that questions aren't the opposite of faith. They live inside faith. Faith is choosing to lean toward what you can't yet prove, because the One you're leaning on is trustworthy.
days.smallAction: Pick one thing you can't yet see proof of. Practice leaning toward it today — one small action.
days.reflectionPrompt: What questions have you been treating as faith-killers? What if they're just questions?

quiz.question: What is faith, according to Hebrews?
options: Substance of things hoped for, evidence of things not seen
quiz.explanation: Substance — something real, weight-bearing — about things not yet visible. Not certainty. Trust.

days.openingPrayer: God, make my faith real in the way I treat people today.

scripture.verseText: For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul is cutting through religious noise. The thing that matters isn't your tribe, your rituals, your performance, or even your beliefs in isolation. It's faith expressing itself through love. Real faith leaks. It shows up in how you treat the person at the checkout, the parent you're frustrated with, the stranger online. If your faith is growing, the people around you should slowly feel it.
days.smallAction: Pick one person today and let your faith show up as a small love — a text, a moment of patience, an undeserved kindness.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where has your faith stayed private when it could have shown up as love this week?

quiz.question: What does Paul say is what matters?
quiz.explanation: Faith working through love. That's the proof of life, not the labels.

days.openingPrayer: God, thank you for fourteen days. Keep going with me.

scripture.verseText: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.

days.practicalMeaning: Two weeks is just the start. What you've been doing here — showing up, asking, listening, sitting in the silence — is the early stretch of what Paul calls a "good work" that God himself started. He'll finish it. That doesn't mean you'll never struggle, doubt, or fall behind. It means the project isn't yours to complete alone. The faithfulness is his. Your part is to keep showing up.
days.smallAction: Look back at what you wrote on day 1. Then write one sentence about what's different now.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's one thing you'll carry forward from these fourteen days?

quiz.question: Who is responsible for finishing the good work?
quiz.explanation: He started it. He'll finish it. Your part is showing up — his is the carrying through.

name: Trusting What I Can't See
description: Fourteen honest days for the doubt-haunted — how to walk forward when you can't see.

chapters.title: Walking into what you can't see

days.openingPrayer: God, this is what I have. Both halves. Take both.

scripture.verseText: And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.

days.practicalMeaning: A father is asking Jesus to heal his son. Jesus says it depends on belief. The father gives the truest prayer ever recorded: "I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both halves at once. He has faith *and* doubt, and he says both out loud. Jesus doesn't scold him for the second half. He heals the son anyway. That's the model. The faith you have is enough. The doubt you have is not disqualifying.
days.smallAction: Today, when doubt hits, say it the way the father said it: "I believe; help my unbelief." Both halves.
days.reflectionPrompt: What part of your doubt have you been hiding because you thought it disqualified you from faith?

quiz.question: How does Jesus respond to the father's mixed-faith prayer?
quiz.explanation: He honored the half-belief. Mixed faith is real faith. The honest prayer counted.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, my faith feels too small to matter. Show me it's enough.

scripture.verseText: And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?

days.practicalMeaning: Peter walks on water for a few steps, then doubts, then starts sinking. Jesus catches him *immediately*. Not after Peter swims back, not after a lecture. Immediately. The phrase "O thou of little faith" sounds like a rebuke; it's also a recognition. Peter has *some* faith — enough to get out of the boat. Little faith is real faith. The hand is already extended.
days.smallAction: When you doubt today, picture Peter sinking — and Jesus's hand already extended. Don't wait until you're stronger. Reach.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where has "my faith is too small" stopped you from reaching for help?

quiz.question: When did Jesus catch Peter?
quiz.explanation: Immediately. The hand was extended before Peter could even ask. Little faith got a full rescue.

days.openingPrayer: God, you're bigger than what I can comprehend. Help me let that be a relief, not a barrier.

scripture.verseText: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.

days.practicalMeaning: Job has spent 37 chapters demanding an explanation from God. When God finally speaks, he doesn't give an explanation — he gives a question. "Where were you when I made the earth?" It sounds harsh, but it's actually a relief. Job doesn't have to understand God to trust him. The bigness that puts our questions in perspective is the same bigness that holds us. A God you could fully understand wouldn't be big enough to be God.
days.smallAction: When you can't understand something today, hold this: "This is bigger than my understanding. That's actually fine."
days.reflectionPrompt: What have you been demanding God explain before you'd trust him? What if the explanation isn't coming, but the holding still is?

quiz.question: What is God's answer to Job's questions?
options: A bigger question about scale and mystery
quiz.explanation: Not an answer — a bigger frame. Trust without full understanding is the only kind there is.

days.openingPrayer: God, my understanding isn't strong enough to direct me. Direct me anyway.

scripture.verseText: Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

days.practicalMeaning: Doubt makes us want a map before a step. Proverbs reverses the order: take the step, then the path gets clearer. "Lean not unto thine own understanding" isn't anti-intellectual — it's anti-paralysis. Your understanding is real, just not load-bearing enough for the whole future. Trust is choosing to take a step before the next one is illuminated.
days.smallAction: Take the smallest possible step today on something you've been waiting to fully understand before acting on.
days.reflectionPrompt: What are you waiting to understand before you'll trust? What if the trust has to come first?

quiz.question: What does Proverbs warn against leaning on?
quiz.explanation: Not because understanding is wrong — because it isn't strong enough on its own to bear the future.

days.themeLabel: Walk by faith, not by sight
days.openingPrayer: God, the sight isn't there today. Faith is what I have. Help me walk on that.

scripture.verseText: For we walk by faith, not by sight.

days.practicalMeaning: Six words. They go against everything modern life trains us into. We want the data, the proof, the visible confirmation. Paul says: that's not the operating system of the Christian life. You walk by faith — meaning you take steps without first being able to see where they land. That's not denial. It's trust that the ground will be there.
days.smallAction: Make one small decision today on faith — without waiting for the full picture.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where in your life have you stopped walking because the sight ran out? What would the next step look like on faith?

quiz.question: How does Paul describe the Christian life?
options: Walking by faith, not by sight
quiz.explanation: By faith, not by sight. The sight comes after the step, not before.

days.openingPrayer: God, help me be faithful in the small things — that's the muscle I'm building.

scripture.verseText: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.

days.practicalMeaning: Trust isn't built in dramatic moments — it's built in small consistent ones. Jesus is making this point: the person you'll be in the big test is the person you've been practicing being all along. Doubt grows in inactivity. Trust grows by being used, in small things, repeatedly. The discipline of small yeses to God now is what carries you when the big questions come.
days.smallAction: Find one small thing today you've been putting off but know is right. Do it. That's the muscle.
days.reflectionPrompt: What small daily yes-to-God have you been avoiding because it felt too small to matter?

quiz.question: What does Jesus link being faithful in small with?
quiz.explanation: The small is the rehearsal for the big. The muscle gets built where no one's watching.

days.openingPrayer: God, anchor me. The waves are loud today.

scripture.verseText: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil.

days.practicalMeaning: Hebrews uses the image of an anchor. An anchor doesn't stop the storm — it stops the drift. Hope doesn't promise the questions go away; it keeps you from drifting where you can't get back from. "Sure and steadfast" — it doesn't move even when you do. You can be unsteady and still anchored. The anchor's job is not to make you steady. It's to be unbreakable.
days.smallAction: When the waves feel loud today, picture the anchor — not in you, but underneath you. It holds whether you feel it or not.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where have you been drifting because you forgot the anchor was already set?

quiz.question: What does the verse say hope is?
quiz.explanation: An anchor. Not a feeling — a structural fact. The hope holds whether you feel held or not.

days.openingPrayer: God, my questions are real. I'm bringing them to you, not around you.

scripture.verseText: How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?

days.practicalMeaning: Psalm 13 is in the Bible. The prayer book of the people of God includes "how long will you forget me?" The honest question is welcome — so welcome that it has its own genre (lament). If you've been editing out the part of your prayers that questions God, you can stop. The Bible already has language for it. Bring the questions to him, not around him.
days.smallAction: Pray one honest question to God today — out loud, in a journal, in your head. The kind you've been editing out.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's the question you've been editing out of your prayers? What if you let it in?

quiz.question: What does Psalm 13 demonstrate?
options: Honest lament is welcome in prayer
God is silent in our doubt
quiz.explanation: Doubt's questions are prayer's language too. The Psalmist gives us permission.

days.themeLabel: God meets us in our questions
days.openingPrayer: Jesus, like Thomas, I want to see. Come anyway.

scripture.verseText: Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.

days.practicalMeaning: Thomas refused to believe Jesus had risen unless he could touch the wounds. Jesus appears — and the first thing he does is offer the wounds. He doesn't shame Thomas for needing evidence. He meets him exactly where he is. The label "doubting Thomas" became an insult; it shouldn't be. Thomas asked the honest question, and Jesus answered it by showing up. The doubt was a door, not a wall.
days.smallAction: Your doubt is not a wall. Pray once today: "Jesus, meet me here." That's the same prayer Thomas prayed.
days.reflectionPrompt: What doubt have you been treating as a wall that Jesus might be ready to walk through?

quiz.question: How does Jesus respond to Thomas's doubt?
options: Shows up and offers his wounds for inspection
Tells him to believe without evidence
quiz.explanation: He met Thomas exactly where Thomas needed meeting. Doubt as door, not wall.

days.openingPrayer: God, the silence is heavy. Be in it.

scripture.verseText: But unto thee have I cried, O Lord; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee. Lord, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?

days.practicalMeaning: Psalm 88 is the darkest in the Bible. There's no resolution. It ends "the darkness is my closest friend." And it's still scripture. That's important. God didn't edit it out for being too bleak. The silence is part of the language of faith. When you pray and feel nothing back, you're not failing. You're praying Psalm 88. The honesty of it is the prayer.
days.smallAction: If God feels silent today, pray Psalm 88's last line: "darkness is my closest friend." Then keep praying anyway. That's the faithfulness.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where have you been treating God's silence as proof of his absence? What if it's just silence?

quiz.question: What's notable about Psalm 88?
options: It's the darkest psalm — and still scripture
It was removed from older Bibles
quiz.explanation: Bleak honesty got kept. The silence and dark are inside scripture's language for faith.

days.openingPrayer: God, when nothing is going right, teach me to rejoice anyway. Not pretending — actually.

scripture.verseText: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation.

days.practicalMeaning: Habakkuk lists everything failing — fig tree, vines, olive, flock, herd. The whole economy is collapsing. Then he says: yet I will rejoice. Not because everything is fine. Because *God* is still God in the wreckage. This is the faith forged in the dark — the kind that doesn't require the situation to improve before it can hold steady. It's not denial. It's rooted somewhere deeper than circumstance.
days.smallAction: Pick one thing that's wrong in your life right now. Say: "This is wrong. *And* God is still God." Both halves.
days.reflectionPrompt: What in your life would you have to release control of to be able to say "yet I will rejoice"?

quiz.question: What does Habakkuk model?
options: Faith only when things go well
Faith that names the loss AND chooses joy in God
quiz.explanation: Honest about the wreckage. Anchored in God despite it. Both halves.

days.openingPrayer: God, take the hard parts of this season and make them something. I can't, but you can.

scripture.verseText: And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope; And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit which is given unto us.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul lays out a chain: tribulation → patience → experience → hope. He's not saying suffering is good. He's saying it's not wasted. The thing that feels like pure loss is, in slow ways you can't see in the moment, building something. Hope, on the back end. The kind that doesn't disappoint, because the love of God was supplied while you weren't watching.
days.smallAction: Notice one thing this hard season is making you. Not what it's taking. What it's making.
days.reflectionPrompt: What might be growing in you because of what you're going through, that you wouldn't have learned any other way?

quiz.question: What is the end of Paul's chain?
quiz.explanation: Hope. The thing that feels lost in tribulation is, in slow ways, building the thing you most need.

days.themeLabel: A lamp, one step at a time
days.openingPrayer: God, just light enough for the next step. I trust you for the rest.

scripture.verseText: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.

days.practicalMeaning: Notice the metaphor: lamp at your feet, light on your path. Not a floodlight on the whole future. Just enough for the next step. We want the whole map; God gives us the lamp. The lamp is enough if all you need to do is walk. Walk. The next step's light will come when you take this step.
days.smallAction: Don't try to plan your whole future today. Take one step that's lit. That's enough.
days.reflectionPrompt: What future-decision-anxiety have you been carrying that today's lamp doesn't actually need to address?

quiz.question: How much light does the verse promise?
options: A floodlight on the whole path
Light only after we pray hard enough
Light when our faith is strong
quiz.explanation: A lamp at your feet. Enough for the next step. The map comes step by step.

days.openingPrayer: God, I will be uneven. Thank you that you aren't.

scripture.verseText: If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul ends fourteen days the way he should. "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful." Your faith will waver. Your belief will have weeks where it disappears entirely. He stays faithful anyway. He can't be otherwise — "he cannot deny himself." The journey of doubt and trust isn't a project of you proving you're consistent enough. It's the slow discovery that he is.
days.smallAction: Look back at day 1. Then write one sentence to your day-1 self about what you've learned to trust.
days.reflectionPrompt: What has shifted in how you hold doubt over these fourteen days?

quiz.question: What happens when our faith wavers?
quiz.explanation: He cannot deny himself. The faithfulness is his nature, not your performance.

name: What's Beneath the Anger
description: Fourteen days to face what's under the anger and let love grow back through it.

days.openingPrayer: God, my anger is real. Help me hold it without letting it hold me.

scripture.verseText: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul doesn't say "don't be angry." He says be angry without sinning. Anger itself isn't sin — it's a signal. Something is wrong, and you noticed. The sin enters when the anger curdles into bitterness, contempt, or retaliation. "Don't let the sun go down on it" is practical: stagnant anger ferments. Catch it before it does.
days.smallAction: Today, when anger rises, name it before reacting. "I'm angry about X." One sentence. Out loud or in your head.
days.reflectionPrompt: What did you notice your anger pointing to today? What was the signal underneath it?

quiz.question: What does Paul say is the line between anger and sin?
options: Anger isn't sin — letting it fester is
Anger toward enemies is fine, others isn't
quiz.explanation: Anger is a signal. Sin enters when you let it stay past its usefulness.

days.openingPrayer: God, give me a longer fuse than I've been carrying.

scripture.verseText: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.

days.practicalMeaning: James orders it: hear first, speak second, anger third. Most of our worst moments invert that — we get angry, speak, then hear. The wrath of man doesn't work the righteousness of God. Translation: hot reactions don't produce the outcomes you actually want. Slow is not weak. Slow is what keeps the relationship intact long enough for the truth to land.
days.smallAction: Once today when you feel anger rising, count to five before responding. Five whole seconds.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where today did speed turn an anger moment into a regret moment?

quiz.question: What's James's recommended order?
options: Listen quickly, speak slowly, anger slowly
quiz.explanation: Listen quickly. Speak slowly. Become angry slowly. The order matters.

days.openingPrayer: God, what is my anger trying to tell me? Help me listen.

scripture.verseText: He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.

days.practicalMeaning: Anger is data, not noise. Behind every angry reaction is something you valued that you felt was threatened, dismissed, or violated. The point isn't to suppress the anger. It's to read what it's revealing. Slow wrath gives you time to read; hasty wrath skips reading and just amplifies whatever folly was nearest.
days.smallAction: Pick one moment of anger from this week. Ask: what was I really protecting? What did I value that felt threatened?
days.reflectionPrompt: What does your most recent anger reveal about what you most love or fear?

quiz.question: What does slow wrath produce?
quiz.explanation: Slow wrath gives time to read what's underneath. That reading is wisdom.

days.openingPrayer: God, I'd rather discharge than sit. Help me sit.

scripture.verseText: Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still.

days.practicalMeaning: The Hebrew here can be translated "tremble and don't sin" — be moved by what moved you, but don't act out. Commune with your own heart in the silence. Anger that's discharged immediately bypasses the most important conversation: the one with yourself about what just happened. Stillness isn't suppression. It's the space where the anger becomes information.
days.smallAction: Tonight before sleep, spend two minutes in silence with one piece of today's anger. Don't fix it. Just sit with it.
days.reflectionPrompt: What does anger want to tell you that you've been too busy reacting to hear?

quiz.question: What does the Psalmist recommend?
options: Commune with your heart, be still
quiz.explanation: Stillness gives anger time to become information instead of just impact.

days.openingPrayer: God, give me wisdom to know what to address and what to release.

scripture.verseText: The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.

days.practicalMeaning: Not every offense needs a response. Some offenses are about you; many are about the other person's bad day, hidden wound, or unaddressed pattern. Wisdom is choosing which battles to fight. "His glory to pass over" — passing things over isn't weakness or doormat-ism. It's the choice of someone secure enough not to need to win this one.
days.smallAction: Pick one minor irritation today that you'd normally let chew on you. Let it pass. Don't reply. Notice what happens.
days.reflectionPrompt: What small offense have you been keeping a tally of that wisdom would let you pass over?

quiz.question: What does the verse call "glory"?
quiz.explanation: Glory is the strength to let it go. Not weakness. Security.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, you put reconciliation before worship. Help me see who I need to find.

scripture.verseText: Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.

days.practicalMeaning: Jesus pauses worship for reconciliation. The vertical relationship with God doesn't move forward over the broken horizontal one with another person. If there's someone you've been avoiding — someone you've wronged or who feels wronged by you — God says the offering can wait. Go find them first. This is one of the most expensive verses in the New Testament, and one of the most freeing.
days.smallAction: Name one person you've been avoiding because of a hard thing between you. Don't fix it today — just acknowledge to yourself who it is.
days.reflectionPrompt: Whose face came to mind just now? What's been keeping you from reaching out?

quiz.question: What does Jesus say to do before bringing a gift to God?
quiz.explanation: Reconciliation comes before worship. The vertical doesn't bypass the horizontal.

days.openingPrayer: God, the bitterness has stayed too long. Help me put it down.

scripture.verseText: Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul lists the spiritual wreckage: bitterness, wrath, clamor, evil speech, malice. The word he uses for "put away" is the same word for taking off clothes. These aren't who you are — they're things you've been wearing. You can take them off. Then he names what to put on instead: kindness, tenderheartedness, forgiveness. The exchange isn't moralism; it's freedom.
days.smallAction: Name one piece of bitterness you've been wearing. Picture taking it off. Notice the difference.
days.reflectionPrompt: What does the bitterness cost you that you've stopped noticing because you've worn it so long?

quiz.question: What's the image Paul uses for getting rid of bitterness?
options: Putting it away — like taking off clothes
quiz.explanation: Clothes. You can take them off. They're not who you are.

days.openingPrayer: God, the urge to even the score is strong. Be stronger than it in me.

scripture.verseText: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.

days.practicalMeaning: Paul says: vengeance isn't yours. Hand it to God. That's not letting the offender off — it's getting yourself out of the loop where their wrong becomes your sin. Then he goes further: feed them. Give them drink. Not because they deserve it. Because not doing it would make you what they were. Overcome evil with good.
days.smallAction: For one person you've been quietly keeping a tally about: do one small kindness today. Even tiny. Not because they deserve it — because you don't want to be them.
days.reflectionPrompt: Whose harm have you been carrying as a debt you intend to collect? What would handing it to God feel like?

quiz.question: Why does Paul tell us not to take vengeance?
options: Because vengeance belongs to God, not us
quiz.explanation: It's not yours to do. Handing it to God frees you from becoming what they were.

days.openingPrayer: Jesus, you forgave me. Let that be the measure, not what they did.

scripture.verseText: Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.

days.practicalMeaning: The standard isn't what they did. It's what you've been forgiven. "Even as Christ forgave you" is a high bar — uncondition al, repeated, costly. The point isn't that forgiving is easy. It's that the math of "what they deserve" gets swallowed by the math of "what I've already received." You forgive from receipt, not from your reserves.
days.smallAction: Picture one moment of grace you've been given. Hold it for thirty seconds. Then think of one person you've been refusing to extend grace to.
days.reflectionPrompt: What forgiveness have you received that should make this one — the one you're holding — feel possible?

quiz.question: What's the standard for forgiving others?
quiz.explanation: Christ's forgiveness sets the bar. You forgive from what you've received, not from your reserves.

days.openingPrayer: God, I want to be forgiven more than I want to be right. Soften me.

scripture.verseText: For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

days.practicalMeaning: This is the hard verse. Jesus draws a direct connection — the door you open to others is the door God opens to you. It's not a contract; it's a mirror. The heart that refuses to release is the same heart that has trouble receiving release. Forgiving someone doesn't earn God's forgiveness. It opens you to it.
days.smallAction: Pray the Lord's Prayer today, slowly. When you reach "forgive us our trespasses as we forgive," pause.
days.reflectionPrompt: What unforgiveness are you holding that might be the same door you've been wishing God would open for you?

quiz.question: What's the connection Jesus draws?
options: The door we open to others is the same we open to ourselves
We must forgive first, then ask
quiz.explanation: Not contract — mirror. The heart that releases is the heart that receives.

days.openingPrayer: God, I've been keeping receipts. Help me burn them.

scripture.verseText: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.

days.practicalMeaning: "Thinketh no evil" — older translations say "keeps no record of wrongs." Love doesn't ledger. We do. Most resentment is just an internal balance sheet we keep running on someone. Love is the courage to close the book. Not deny what happened — close the book. The relationship can't grow forward as long as the ledger keeps growing backward.
days.smallAction: Pick one grievance you've been keeping. Today, decide: I'm closing the book on this one.
days.reflectionPrompt: What ledger have you been maintaining that's been keeping a relationship frozen?

quiz.question: What does love NOT do, according to Paul?
quiz.explanation: Love closes the book on the ledger. The relationship can grow once the ledger stops.

days.openingPrayer: God, today I choose to refrain. Strengthen the choice.

scripture.verseText: Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil.

days.practicalMeaning: "Fret not" is interesting — anger and fretting are linked. The Hebrew "fret" carries a sense of self-heating, getting yourself worked up by replaying. The Psalmist sees what we do: we feed the anger by going back over it. Cease, forsake, stop fretting. The fretting is the fuel. Pulling it shrinks the fire.
days.smallAction: When you catch yourself replaying an anger moment today, gently say "I don't have to keep feeding this" and let it go for now.
days.reflectionPrompt: What anger moment have you been replaying like a movie? What would shutting off the projector feel like?

quiz.question: What does "fret" link to in this Psalm?
quiz.explanation: Fretting is the fuel for anger. Cut the fuel; the fire shrinks.

days.openingPrayer: God, give me the strength of restraint today.

scripture.verseText: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.

days.practicalMeaning: Slow anger is stronger than physical might. Self-rule is greater than conquering cities. The metaphor is ancient but the point is timeless: external strength matters less than internal mastery. The person who can hold their fire when provoked is doing harder, rarer work than the person who wins external battles. Most of us want to be that person — Proverbs says you can be.
days.smallAction: Today, in one moment where reaction is automatic, choose restraint instead. Notice the strength it took.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where in your life has restraint been mistaken for weakness? What if it was actually the harder strength?

quiz.question: What does Proverbs call stronger than military victory?
quiz.explanation: Ruling your spirit is greater than taking a city. The internal mastery is the rarer strength.

days.openingPrayer: God, take what you've made and pour it back through me. Make me kind.

scripture.verseText: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.

days.practicalMeaning: Fourteen days end with the simplest instruction: be kind. After everything — the anger named, the bitterness released, the forgiveness practiced — what remains is kindness. Tenderness. The soft heart that's been earned through hard work. This is the freedom from anger isn't a colder version of you. It's the warmest version, finally able to hold others without fortifying yourself.
days.smallAction: Find one person today and let kindness lead. Not because they deserve it. Because you're freer than you used to be.
days.reflectionPrompt: Who in your life would feel the difference if the version of you they met tomorrow was the version this path is forming?

quiz.question: What does freedom from anger look like?
quiz.explanation: Warmer, not colder. The hard work makes the soft heart possible.

name: Saying the Hard Thing
description: Fourteen days to learn the art of saying the true thing, with love, when it matters most.

days.openingPrayer: God, the truth and the love both. Don't let me trade one for the other.

scripture.verseText: But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.

days.practicalMeaning: Two errors in conversation: the cowardly love that won't say the true thing, and the brutal truth that doesn't bother to love. Paul says: both. Truth without love is just cruelty wearing a religious mask. Love without truth is sentimentality that lets the relationship die slowly. The mature work is the harder middle: say it true, say it kind, mean both.
days.smallAction: Think of one hard truth you've been avoiding because you're afraid it'll feel unkind. Hold it for a minute and ask: how do I say it true AND kind?
days.reflectionPrompt: Which side do you usually fall to — truth without love, or love without truth?

quiz.question: What does Paul require together?
quiz.explanation: Both. Truth without love is cruelty; love without truth is decay. The middle is the work.

days.openingPrayer: God, give me friends who'll tell me hard things — and make me one.

scripture.verseText: Open rebuke is better than secret love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

days.practicalMeaning: A friend who tells you the truth that hurts is doing more for you than someone who privately loves you while letting you walk into a wall. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" — friend-wounds are *trustworthy*. They're trying to save you. Enemy-kisses (flattery, agreement, conflict-avoidance) feel kinder in the moment but they're not faithful. They're convenient.
days.smallAction: Identify one person in your life who tells you hard truths. Thank them today — text, call, in person. They're doing trustworthy work.
days.reflectionPrompt: Who in your life is faithful enough to wound you with truth? Who in your life are you that person for?

quiz.question: What does Proverbs call friend-wounds?
quiz.explanation: Faithful. Wounds from a real friend are trying to save you. They're trustworthy.

days.openingPrayer: God, give me the wisdom to know when. Then the courage to do it.

scripture.verseText: A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.

days.practicalMeaning: Not every conversation belongs to today. Wisdom is partly knowing when. "A time to keep silence" — not forever, just for now. The silence that's preparing the right time is faithful. The silence that's avoiding is not. Both look the same from outside. You can tell from inside which one you're in.
days.smallAction: Identify one conversation you've been postponing. Honestly ask: is this faithful waiting or fearful avoiding? Don't decide yet — just notice which one it is.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's the difference for you between waiting for the right moment and avoiding the moment altogether?

quiz.question: What's the wisdom in Ecclesiastes about silence?
options: There's a time to keep silent AND a time to speak
quiz.explanation: Both have a time. Knowing which time it is, is the wisdom.

days.openingPrayer: God, before I speak today, help me actually hear.

scripture.verseText: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.

days.practicalMeaning: James gives the order: hear first. Speak second. Anger third. Most hard conversations go badly because we invert this — we arrive with our point loaded and listen only enough to find the gap to insert it. Real listening means letting the other person be more real to you, more complete, than they were when you started. That alone changes the conversation.
days.smallAction: In your next conversation today, listen to the other person fully before responding. Don't pre-draft your reply. Just listen.
days.reflectionPrompt: When did you last fully listen to someone without forming your response? How was the conversation different?

quiz.question: What's James's order?
quiz.explanation: Listen first. Speak second. Anger slowly. The order is the discipline.

days.openingPrayer: God, slow my response. Quiet the urgency.

scripture.verseText: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.

days.practicalMeaning: Proverbs is blunt: it's folly to answer before you've heard. We do this constantly — we hear two sentences and jump to conclusions about what the other person is saying, then respond to a version of them we made up. The shame in this is real. The fix is small: ask one more question before responding. Just one.
days.smallAction: In any hard conversation today, ask one more clarifying question before you respond. "Can you say more about that?"
days.reflectionPrompt: When did you last answer based on a version of someone you'd assembled rather than what they were actually saying?

quiz.question: What does Proverbs call answering before hearing?
quiz.explanation: Folly and shame. Both. The fix: ask one more question.

days.themeLabel: Fools delight in their own opinion
days.openingPrayer: God, help me hold my view loosely enough to learn.

scripture.verseText: A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself.

days.practicalMeaning: Proverbs draws a line: a fool isn't interested in understanding the other person — they're interested in revealing themselves.
